background.definition: Body lice are parasitic insects that live on the body and in the clothing or bedding of infested humans. Pubic lice are parasitic insects found in the genital area of humans, while head lice are parasitic insects found on the heads of people.

list.listitem: According to the National Institutes of Health, approximately 3 million people in the United States are infected annually with pubic lice.

A systematic review of 39 studies with 105,383 primary school children in low and middle income countries found a pooled prevalence of 20.0% (95% CI 14.0 to 25.9%). Being a girl (aOR 3.7) and having a previous infestation (aOR 4.5) were risk factors.
While there is a stigma associated with head lice, it is not related to poor hygiene.
Body lice are more common among people who live in crowded conditions or have decreased access to personal hygeine and clean clothes such as homeless individuals or refugees.
Pediculus humanus capitis is the agent causing head lice infestations.
Pediculus humanus humanus is the agent causing body lice infestations.
Phthirus pubis is the agent causing pediculosis pubis (pubic lice) infestations.
Pediculosis pubis is usually transmitted by sexual contact.
Body and head lice infestations are usually transmitted by direct contact or use of a contaminated object (clothing, hat, brush, etc.).
Body lice are associated with poor hygiene and homelessness.

list.listitem: Patients usually complain of itching of scalp, nape of neck, or pubic area. Take history of suspected or confirmed cases among close contacts (family member, classmate) or any recent case of active head lice.
Visualization of the live adults or nymphs in the hair is diagnostic of infestation with head or pubic lice.
Nits can be seen in active disease or treated disease. Nits closer to the scalp are newer and more likely to contain live unhatched lice.
Visualization of the live adult or nymphs in clothing is diagnostic of body lice infestation.
Wet combing has been shown to improve detection of head lice.
Diagnosis is clinical; culture or biopsy is not recommended unless the diagnosis is unclear.

Head lice: finding nits without an adult louse does not mean that the infestation has resolved. Look for nits and lice in the hair, especially at the nape of the neck, behind the ears, and above the ears. There are many more nits present than live adults.
Body lice: look for the lice and larvae in the seams of the clothing.

Pubic lice: little specks of dried blood may be seen in the underwear as a clue to the infestation. Look for nits and lice on the pubic hairs. These lice and their nits may also be seen on the hairs of the upper thighs, abdomen, and eyelashes.

Pediculicides are generally equivalent, and the choice among malathion, permethrin, and pyrethrin is based on local resistance patterns as permethrin resistance in particular is very common (.
Retreatment in 7-10 days may be necessary if lice are found or if eggs are observed at the hair-skin junction.
Retreat patients who do not respond to initial treatment with an alternative regimen.
Topical treatment with 0.5% ivermectin is a safe and effective treatment for head lice, but is expensive. Oral ivermectin is another option with comparable efficacy.

Topical occlusive therapies like silicone oils (eg, dimeticone) and petrolatum may be as effective or more effective than pediculicides, with minimal adverse effects. A systematic review of 17 RCTs found low-certainty evidence that topical occlusive agents are better than pediculocides in terms of final cure rate (RR 1.20, 95% CI 1.02-1.41), with no difference in adverse events such as skin and eye irritation (RR 0.65, 95% CI 0.36-1.17). Dimeticone, a silicone that eradicates lice by occluding and blocking its excretory system, appears more effective than permethrin and malathion, and does not seem to be affected by resistance unlike pediculocides.

Isopropyl myristate, which works as an occlusive agent or by dissolving lice cuticle wax, appears more effective than pediculocides like malathion, permethrin, and pyrethrum, based on low-certainty evidence.

A single application of abametapir 0.74% lotion (Xeglyze) for 10 minutes appears to be more effective than vehicle in treating head lice in two identical phase III clinical trials (81.1% success vs. 50.9%, P=0.001 in 1 trial; 81.8% vs 47.2%, P<0.001 in the other trial). Abametapir works by chelating heavy metal cations causing inhibition of metalloproteinases necessary for ova development, hatching, and adult survival. It has been FDA-approved for patients 6 months and older.

Limited evidence supports the use of trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole orally twice a day for 10 days. It is postulated to kill the symbiotic bacteria in the gut of the louse. Consider combination therapy with 1% permethrin and trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole in cases of multiple treatment failures.
Plant extracts and essential oils (eg, eucalyptus oil, tea tree oil, tocopheryl acetate) are widely available treatment options in Australia. Evidence is insufficient to support their efficacy.
Bedding and clothing should be decontaminated (ie, machine-washed and machine-dried using the heat cycle, or dry cleaned) or removed from body contact for at least 72 hours.
Improved hygiene and clean clothes is typically sufficient for managment of pediculosis corporis (body lice).
Fumigation of living areas is not necessary.
Studies regarding physical treatment methods such as combing with a wet fine-toothed comb ("Bug-Busting") have had mixed results.
Patients with bacterial superinfections may need oral antibiotics.
With adequate treatment of the infestation and the personal items containing the lice (clothing, bed linens, hair brush, etc.), complete resolution is expected. C
Evaluate patients with lice after 1 to 2 weeks if symptoms persist. Retreatment may be necessary if lice are found or if eggs are observed at the hair-skin junction. C
Make an effort to comb out all remaining nits on the hair.
Make sure that all infested contacts are treated to avoid recurrences in families, schools, and shelters.
If a live louse is found after treatment is completed, retreatment of the patient and all close contacts will be needed.
Treat pregnant and lactating women with either a fine-toothed comb, permethrin, or pyrethrins with piperonyl butoxide.
Lindane is contraindicated in pregnancy and lactation.
Avoid lindane because of its neurotoxicity.

feature.caption: Treatment Options for Lice.
feature.feature_body:
Drug Directions
Permethrin 1% cream rinse Apply to affected areas and wash off after 10 min
Pyrethrins with piperonyl butoxide Apply to affected areas and wash off after 10 min
Malathion 0.5% lotion Apply for 8-12 h and wash off
Ivermectin 0.2 mg/kg Give once orally and repeat in 2 wk for head lice
Ivermectin 0.25 mg/kg Give once orally and repeat in 2 wk for pubic lice
Spinosad 0.9% suspension Apply to affected areas and wash off after 10 min
